## IX Limitations and Threats to Validity

Below I describe all the limitations and threats to the validity of the evaluation and development of SideKernel. The majority of those limitations are attributed to the time constraints of the practicum (which required scoping down), and single-evaluator bias.

• 

Evaluator bias. The comparative analysis unavoidably introduces bias, because the developer is also the evaluator. Although I took every reasonable measure to reduce it (e.g. fixed success criteria, binary outcomes based on built-in capabilities,
auditable tests, standardized and transparent friction notes), a better
methodology would involve multiple users, something, however, practically
infeasible within the practicum’s timeline.

• 

User survey instrument bias. The user survey instrument is designed by the developer. Many of the survey’s questions are multiple-choice or multi-select format. This anchors respondents towards the pre-formulated options, which introduces bias. I mitigate this by providing a free-text “Other” option on closed questions, as well as enriching the instrument with open free-text questions. While this likely reduces the instrument bias, it does not eliminate it.

• 

Sampling bias. The online survey’s sample tilts towards a security-aware audience. Real-world AI coding agent sandbox adoption is therefore probably significantly lower than the 38.2% that the study records.

• 

Sample size. While the sample (N = 80 respondents; 33 current or former sandbox users) is likely sufficient for formative/directional signals, it is low. The results were used for informed development decisions and a framework for the comparative analysis, rather than statistically generalizable data.

• 

Informal study status. The formative user survey was conducted as informal practicum research and did not undergo a formal Georgia Tech IRB review. The study is not designed to produce generalizable knowledge but rather its results are interpreted as signals for the development and evaluation of SideKernel, rather than rigorous academic data.

• 

Usability is measured indirectly. The tests measure how well a sandbox addresses the survey’s usability barriers, not usability in any general sense.

• 

Binary scoring without gradation. The binary score of the capability tests is blind to friction. While I remediate this with qualitative notes on friction, it does not eliminate the fact that the score itself does not weigh the very nuances that describe usability.

• 

Binary scoring without weights. The binary score of the capability tests does not consider which capabilities are important for the users in practice. The scores are naive, in the sense that the binary outcomes are unweighted. Therefore, the results are approximations.
